paper_title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in video generation have made automated advertising production increasingly feasible. However, an effective advertisement must faithfully represent the product and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling, which requires more than visual synthesis: it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about a product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. In this paper, we introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation, transforming concise creative briefs into finished advertisements. Our multimodal agent autonomously researches products through web and image search and translates its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator. To achieve this, we develop a dedicated data construction pipeline that yields two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, and train the agent through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with joint optimization of storyboard- and video-level rewards. We further introduce AdCreation-Bench, comprising 305 advertising briefs across eight domains, with two complementary metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising effectiveness assessed by an independent judge. Experiments demonstrate that AdProducer improves the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3 and generalizes to Veo 3.1 without additional training, improving its score from 28.0 to 35.9, with consistent gains in Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations. Code, models, and data are released.

Code, models, and data are fully released. 1. Introduction Recent advances in video generation have enabled the synthesis of highly realistic videos from text prompts and visual references [2, 10, 25, 27, 30, 32, 33, 37, 47, 48, 55], opening new opportunities for automated advertising production [21, 22, 64]. However, while conventional video generation primarily emphasizes visual quality and prompt alignment, advertising requires understanding what makes product worth promoting and how to communicate its value through compelling visual storytelling [51, 54, 68]. Consider creating an advertisement for newly released foldable smartphone, as illustrated in Fig. 1. visually appealing video may still depict the wrong device, present incorrect specifications, or fail to showcase the folding experience that distinguishes the product. These failures highlight three key challenges in advertising video generation: preserving product identity, ensuring factual correctness, and translating selling points into meaningful visual demonstrations that convey product value [7, 42, 56]. Addressing these challenges requires more than powerful video generators; it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. Recent advances in multimodal agents have demonstrated their potential for complex reasoning and tool use [8, 60], offering promising direction for integrating these capabilities. This motivates us to explore whether multimodal agent can learn to autonomously research products and design compelling advertising storyboards that guide frozen video generator to produce advertisements from concise creative briefs. To this end, we introduce AdProducer, an end-to-end agentic framework that transforms concise briefs into advertising videos through autonomous product research and Figure 2. (a) Traditional advertising workflow vs. (b) AdProducer. AdProducer automates product research and creative planning, enabling rapid advertising video creation from short brief. creative storyboard design (Fig. 2b). To address the scarcity of training data, we develop dedicated data construction pipeline. We first curate advertising briefs spanning 60 product categories across eight domains, then employ teacher agent to conduct multi-round web and image searches. Grounded in the retrieved evidence and visual references, the teacher constructs selling-point-driven storyboards specifying shot content, timing, and camera movements. We subsequently filter the generated trajectories through structural and factual verification and render the storyboards into reference videos using MiniMax H3 [43]. This pipeline produces two training datasets, AdProducerSFT and AdProducer-RL, alongside AdCreation-Bench, held-out benchmark comprising 305 advertising briefs. We further introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising quality and effectiveness, assessed by an independent judge. Building on these datasets, we adopt two-stage training strategy consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) [38, 39]. SFT equips the agent with product research and creative storyboard design capabilities through teacher trajectory imitation, while RL further refines its decision-making through reward optimization. However, video-only rewards can provide noisy feedback due to the limitations of the underlying generator, whereas storyboard-only rewards cannot assess how effectively the planned content is realized. To address these limitations, we jointly optimize storyboardand video-level rewards, providing complementary feedback on creative design and its visual realization. Extensive experiments on AdCreation-Bench demonstrate that AdProducer substantially improves advertising video generation. With the video generator frozen and only the agent trained, AdProducer raises the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3, with strong gains in visual correctness, factual accuracy, and selling-point demonstration. Without retraining, the agent then transfers directly to Veo 3.1 [12], improving its PG-Score from 28.0 to 35.9. Figure 3. Inference trajectory of AdProducer on benchmark brief. The agent verifies product facts through text searches (T1T2), selects visual references through image searches (T3T4), and finally writes selling-point-driven, three-shot storyboard (T5). Only the storyboard and reference images (P1P3) are passed to frozen reference-to-video generator. Prompt and storyboard details are in Sec. A.2. Evaluations using Ad-Score and VideoScore2 [17], together with human studies, further demonstrate improvements in advertising effectiveness and product fidelity, alongside competitive visual quality. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation from concise briefs, which integrates autonomous product research with selling-point-driven storyboard design. We develop two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, to address training data scarcity in agentic advertising video generation, and introduce AdCreation-Bench with PG-Score and Ad-Score to evaluate product correctness and advertising effectiveness. Experiments on AdCreation-Bench show that AdProducer substantially improves product correctness and selling-point presentation with MiniMax H3 and further generalizes to Veo 3.1 without retraining. Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations also confirm gains in advertising effectiveness and visual quality. 2. Related Work Advertising Generation. Prior work on advertising generation has primarily focused on images, exploring controllable layouts, product fidelity, and personalization [5, 9, 35, 50, 63]. Advertising video generation [3, 65] introduces additional challenges in maintaining product consistency and factual accuracy across shots while effectively demonstrating selling points. Existing video-oriented studies have explored advertisement understanding and evaluation [20, 40, 68, 72]. However, end-to-end automated advertising video generation for real-world products remains relatively underexplored. In contrast, our work integrates autonomous product research with storyboard design to generate advertising videos directly from concise creative briefs. Agentic Systems. LLM-based agents leverage multi-step reasoning and tool use to tackle complex, knowledgeintensive tasks [4, 26, 31, 34, 57, 58, 60, 69, 75]. Recent works have extended agentic approaches to image generation through knowledge retrieval and iterative refinement [8, 24, 73], and to multi-shot video generation through script planning, storyboarding, and scene-level coordination [29, 36, 52, 59, 61, 62, 66, 71]. In advertising, existing agentic approaches primarily explore reward-guided video generation using business feedback and quality signals [3]. In contrast, our work focuses on autonomous product research and selling-point-driven storyboard design, enabling advertising video generation from concise briefs. 3. Method 3.1. Overview Given concise creative brief b, AdProducer aims to enable end-to-end advertising video generation, automatically transforming users request into finished advertisement without manual intervention. To achieve this, we introduce multimodal agent πθ that autonomously researches the target product, gathers visual references, and develops structured multi-shot storyboard with selected reference images. frozen video generator then renders the storyboard into the final advertisement v. The agents interleaved reasoning and tool use form trajectory τ πθ( b), which culminates in the storyboard and its selected reference images. The agent iteratively reasons over gathered evidence to determine its next actions, using three tools: search to identify products and verify facts, browse to examine relevant webpages with Gemini 3.1 Pro [13], and image search to retrieve product-specific visual references. Based on the collected evidence, the agent designs structured storyboard  (Fig. 3)  specifying shot timing, visual content, camera movements, and reference assignments. This evidence-grounded design preserves product identity across shots, ensures accurate on-screen text, and shows selling points through visual actions. 3.2. Training Two-Stage Training. We initialize AdProducer from Qwen3.5-9B [46] and adopt two-stage training strategy. We first perform supervised fine-tuning on AdProducerSFT, teaching the agent to conduct multi-round product research, select visual references, and design selling-pointdriven storyboards by imitating teacher trajectories. We then further optimize the agent on AdProducer-RL through reinforcement learning, encouraging more effective tool use and creative decision-making beyond teacher imitation. Throughout training, the video generator remains frozen, and only the multimodal agent is optimized. Joint Reward Design. Directly evaluating generated advertisements provides feedback on the final outcome, but can be unreliable, as video quality depends not only on the agents decisions but also on the limitations and stochasticity of the frozen video generator. Conversely, evaluating storyboards alone cannot determine whether the planned content is faithfully realized in the final video. To address these complementary limitations, we introduce joint reward that considers both video and storyboard quality. We first render each storyboard using the frozen generator and compute the video reward Rvideo = PG(v) (Eq. (4)), assessing how effectively the planned content is realized in the final advertisement. To complement this outcome-based feedback, we employ Gemini 3.1 Pro to evaluate the storyboard and selected references against the brief, verified product facts, official images, and reference video. The judge assesses product identity, factual correctness, required on-screen text, and selling-point demonstration, while considering shot feasibility and narrative coherence. Training Data Construction Training an agent for end-to-end advertising generation requires data that capture the complete workflow of product research, visual reference selection, and storyboard design. However, existing datasets rarely provide such multistep trajectories. To address this gap, we develop fourstage data construction pipeline  (Fig. 4)  that produces highFigure 5. AdCreation-Bench overview. (a) 305 briefs over eight domains, covering broad time span from 1836 to 2026. (b) Example items across different categories and release times, each with brief excerpt, key product facts and the selling point to demonstrate. quality training data through multi-round information retrieval, evidence verification, and storyboard construction. ① Product Briefs Construction. We select products from eight advertising domains spanning 60 categories: consumer electronics, fashion and accessories, food and beverage, beauty and personal care, home and lifestyle, automotive and mobility, travel destinations, and anime and IP merchandise. These domains require diverse visual presentations, from demonstrating product functionality to highlighting material textures and showcasing destinations. For each product, we use Gemini 3.8 Flash [14], equipped with web and image search, to construct creative brief specifying the product, key selling point suitable for 10-second advertisement, and factual requirements without revealing their values. We additionally collect sourcebacked fact table, distinguishing attributes for disambiguating similar products, and two to five official reference images. These supporting materials remain hidden from the agent and are used exclusively for verification, filtering (③ and ④), reward computation, and evaluation. ② Teacher Trajectory Generation. We employ Gemini 3.8 Flash [14] as the teacher agent, which receives only the constructed brief and system prompt and operates with the same tools and budget as the student agent (Sec. 3.1). During multi-round web and image searches, the teacher progressively gathers product evidence, evaluates the relevance of retrieved images, and determines how to translate product features into compelling visual presentations. Each retrieved image is retained or discarded with justification and, when selected, assigned to corresponding shot. Once the research is complete, the teacher constructs the storyboard in the final turn, grounded in the retrieved evidence. The storyboard binds each recurring subject to its reference images and specifies timed sequence of at least three shots over the 10-second ad, each with its composition, action, camera movement, referenced images, and onscreen text. Its design follows advertising conventions: the first shot captures attention, the middle shots visibly demonstrate the selling point rather than merely showing the product, and the final shot leaves memorable product impression, with all on-screen text quoting verified facts (examples in Fig. 3 and Sec. A). These trajectories preserve the reasoning, tool calls, and observations behind each storyboard. ③ Trajectory Verification and Filtering. To ensure the quality and reliability of the collected trajectories, we adopt two-stage filtering process, consisting of an initial validation during data collection and subsequent verification using Claude Opus 5.5 [1]. Specifically, we combine rulebased checks with model-based verification to identify invalid tool calls, missing or mismatched visual references, and storyboards that fail to meet the required output format. We further assess product consistency by comparing selected reference images against official product images, filtering out trajectories that retrieve incorrect products or variants. Through this process, we retain high-quality trajectories that satisfy structural requirements and maintain factual and visual consistency with the target products. ④ Reference Video Generation. To provide visual references for reinforcement learning and benchmark evaluation, we employ the frozen MiniMax H3 video generator [43] to synthesize advertising videos from the verified storyboards. Since the generated videos may contain visual or factual inaccuracies, we assess product fidelity and factual correctness against official product images and annotated facts, rather than relying solely on the synthesized videos. After verification and filtering, we retain 4,710 valid samples comprising 3,710 trajectories for supervised fine-tuning (AdProducerfrom 5,000 training candidates, reinforcement learning SFT) and 1,000 examples for (AdProducer-RL). We additionally curate AdCreationBench, comprising 305 briefs selected from 500 candidates, with no product overlap between training and evaluation sets (details in Sec. 5). 5. AdCreation-Bench Existing video generation benchmarks primarily focus on visual fidelity and temporal consistency [18, 19, 74]. However, visually appealing video does not necessarily make an effective advertisement: it must also faithfully represent the advertised product, convey accurate information, and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling. To evaluate these requirements, we introduce AdCreation-Bench, which consists of creative briefs with verified product annotations (Sec. 5.1) and two complementary metrics, PG-Score for product correctness and Ad-Score for advertising effectiveness (Sec. 5.2). 5.1. Benchmark Construction Following the pipeline in Sec. 4, we curate 305 evaluation samples, each featuring unique product with no overlap with training data. To assess different product knowledge challenges, we organize the benchmark Fig. 5 into three groups: recent (122), comprising products released between July and October 2026, after the models knowledge cutoffs; long-tail (130), covering less-prominent or sparsely documented products released from 1903 to 2026, including older products reassigned from the recent group after launch-date verification; and evergreen (53), focusing on lesser-known component-level details or secondary specifications of widely recognized products released from 1876 to 2022. Each brief requires median of six factual details to be retrieved, and 92% of samples require accurate onscreen text. For briefs without required on-screen text, the text accuracy term is excluded and the remaining weights are renormalized. All reference videos undergo verification by Gemini 3.1 Pro [13] and human inspection. 5.2. Evaluation Metrics PG-Score. We introduce the Product-Grounding Score to evaluate generated advertising videos rather than intermediate storyboards. We employ Gemini 3.1 Pro [13] as multimodal judge to assess the generated videos against the brief, hidden factual annotations, official product images, and reference video that serves as an aesthetic reference. PG-Score comprises five dimensions: visual correctness (vis), measuring product identity and appearance; text accuracy (txt), assessing factual correctness of on-screen text; selling point (sell), measuring visual demonstration of product benefits; shot design (shot), assessing composition and coherence; and aesthetics (aes), evaluating overall visual quality. Each dimension is scored on discrete scale within [0, 1], and the overall score is computed as: PG(v) = 0.4qvis +0.2qtxt +0.2qsell +0.1qshot +0.1qaes. (4) Ad-Score. PG-Score evaluates video mainly from the product side, i.e., whether the product is correctly presented and its selling points are demonstrated. good advertisement, however, should also be judged as whole from the viewers perspective: whether it captures attention, tells coherent story, and persuades the audience. We therefore introduce the Advertising Quality Score (Ad-Score), which assesses overall advertising quality from viewer-oriented perspective. Its dimensions are distilled from the criteria by which advertisements are commonly evaluated in the advertising industry and research [51, 54, 56], and are organized into three groups: brief fidelity and product presentation (brief and product); visual quality and narrative flow (craft); and hook, creative quality, persuasiveness, and purchase intent (advertising effectiveness). Ad-Score is computed by separate judge, GPT-6 Sol [45], which is not involved in training and has no access to the reference video. Given the generated video, creative brief, verified product facts, and official images, the judge rates each dimension on an anchored 15 scale and assigns holistic 110 score, which we report as the AdScore instead of averaging the dimension scores. Together, PG-Score and Ad-Score evaluate whether an advertisement is both faithful to the product and effective for its viewers. 6. Experiments 6.1. Experimental Setup Implementation Details. We train AdProducer with SFT (learning rate 1 105, batch size 16) on 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. RL is conducted on 4 H100 GPUs with learning rate of 1 106, sampling = 6 trajectories per brief with 8 briefs per step, while another 4 H100 GPUs serve MiniMax H3 for video generation. Each trajectory is limited to 8 tool calls (at most 2 image searches, each returning up to 5 images), 6K tokens per turn, and 64K-token context; trajectories exceeding these limits are truncated. The browse tool is powered by Gemini 3.1 Pro. At inference, we use temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.9. Veo 3.1 generates 720p videos, while other generators produce 10-second 480p videos, all in 16:9 without audio. Baselines. We compare AdProducer with state-of-theart video generators that are directly prompted with the brief: the proprietary Veo 3.1 family (Lite, Fast, and standard) [12], and the open-source CogVideoX1.5-5B [67], HunyuanVideo-13B [28], LTX-2-19B [15], Mochi-110B [11], Wan2.2-T2V-A14B [55], and MiniMax H3 [43]. AdProducer consistently improves advertising video quality across different video generators, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability.

Overall, all methods follow the same protocol for fair comparison: each takes creative brief as input and outputs an advertising video for evaluation. Evaluation. We evaluate all methods with the two metrics of AdCreation-Bench (Sec. 5.2): PG-Score, which assesses product correctness and selling-point demonstration against verified annotations, and Ad-Score, which assesses overall advertising quality from viewer-oriented perspective. If AdProducers output fails the strict format check, we fall back to lenient check and, if that also fails, to the baseline brief-to-video generation. We further conduct human study following the absolute category rating (ACR) protocol of ITU-T P.910 [23], in which participants rate the videos of five methods on eight briefs from five domains (40 clips). Each clip is shown alone with its brief and an official product image; method names are hidden, the order is randomized per participant, and repeated clips serve as attention checks. The questionnaire adopts established measures from advertising research and rates five dimensions on labelled five-point scales: visual quality (the ACR scale), product fidelity, informativeness, i.e., whether the ad conveys the products key features [6], attitude toward the ad [41, 44], and purchase intention [53]. Together, these dimensions cover both whether the product is shown correctly and how the advertisement is perceived by viewers. We report mean opinion scores and measure inter-rater agreement with Krippendorffs α [16]. Finally, we report VideoScore2 [17] as complementary check of visual quality, text-video alignment, and physical plausibility, verifying that optimizing for advertising does not degrade video quality. 6.2. Grounded in product research, AdProducer depicts each product as it really looks, presents verified facts as legible on-screen text, and unfolds the selling point across multiple shots with varied compositions. Detailed analysis in Sec. 6.4. Qwen agents under two workflows: planning-only, which explicitly guides selling-point reasoning and storyboard construction without external tools, and search-enabled, which additionally enables product research and visual reference retrieval. Planning-only agents achieve reasonable selling-point and shot-design scores but struggle with visual correctness. Search further improves product grounding (e.g., 34.7 for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B). In contrast, our trained 9B agent achieves 51.3, substantially outperforming both its untrained counterpart (+27.5) and larger untrained models (+16.6 over the best). These results highlight the importance of task-specific training beyond carefully designed prompts, external tool access, and model scaling. Joint Reward Ablation. We examine the contributions of storyboard and video rewards to RL optimization (Tab. 6). SFT substantially improves PG-Score from 17.3 to 48.4. Further RL optimization with storyboard-only or videoonly reward adds only 1.11.3 points, while combining both achieves the best overall PG-Score of 51.3 (+2.9 points over SFT). Removing either reward also lowers sellingpoint demonstration (71.6 to 68.8 and 67.6). This suggests that storyboard feedback supports factual grounding and creative planning, while video feedback assesses how effectively these plans are realized, jointly providing complementary signals for agent optimization. Visual Analysis. Directly prompted baselines mostly produce look-alikes of the official products in Fig. 6; e.g., LTX2 renders N`adar Gin as an amber bottle with red label, whereas the official bottle, reproduced by AdProducer, is clear with green hand-lettered label. Baseline text is also often garbled (CogVideoX), while AdProducer shows the verified 1.54 kg CO2e per bottle. Beyond product correctness, AdProducer organizes its shots around the selling point. For N`adar Gin, sold on net-negative carbon footprint from nitrogen-fixing legumes, the shots move from pea crops to copper stills, the carbon figure, and the bottle, tracing raw material to product. For the Sisley eye cream, sold on de-puffing with cold massage tool, the shots show the jar and tool, the cream texture, and the tool gliding under the eye. Baselines instead hold one static view. 7. Conclusion We presented AdProducer, an end-to-end agentic framework that transforms concise creative briefs into advertising videos through autonomous product research and creative storyboard design. AdProducer improves the PGScore from 17.3 to 51.3 on our AdCreation-Bench, with particularly strong gains in product fidelity, factual accuracy, and recently released products. Its effectiveness further generalizes to Veo 3.1 and is supported by independent model-based and human evaluations.

sections.title: Direct prompt
sections.content: Make 10-second silent video ad for the compact handheld gimbal camera launched by DJI in spring 2026. The video must visually highlight its core selling point of ultra-smooth handheld cinematic stabilization powered by its integrated motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal. Visually and textually verify the exact image sensor size, the maximum 4K high-frame-rate recording capability, the built-in onboard storage capacity, and the physical rotatable touchscreen dimensions and peak brightness, ensuring the device hardware and gimbal mechanism correctly match the verified specifications.

sections.content: subject definitions: <Subject 1> is the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 handheld gimbal camera, featuring compact matte dark-grey chassis with an embossed OSMO lower handle grip, printed white POCKET 4 marking on its left flank, miniature analog joystick and recording controls, an integrated motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal assembly, 1-inch CMOS camera head, and physical 2.0-inch rotatable OLED touchscreen capable of rotating between vertical and horizontal orientations, as shown in <Picture 1>, <Picture 2>, and <Picture 3>. summary: [reference generation] sleek, high-energy 10-second commercial ad highlighting the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 compact handheld gimbal camera launched in spring 2026, demonstrating its core selling point of ultra-smooth handheld cinematic stabilization powered by its integrated motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal, verified 1-inch CMOS sensor, 4K/240fps recording, 107 GB onboard storage, and 2.0-inch 1,000-nit rotatable touchscreen. retention analysis: <Subject 1> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 2], [Shot 3]): fully preserved - Preserves the exact form factor, matte dark-grey chassis, 3-axis motorized mechanical gimbal architecture, 1-inch CMOS camera head, 2.0-inch rotatable touchscreen, joystick controls, and OSMO / POCKET 4 markings. detailed description: The commercial is filmed in crisp, high-contrast cinematic digital style with rich natural contrast, vibrant reflections, and polished studio and goldenhour outdoor lighting. [Shot 1] The commercial opens with an extreme macro close-up pushing slowly in toward <Subject 1>, spotlighted under pristine studio rim lighting against deep slate background. The device powers on as its motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal comes to life, the three miniature brushless motors silently spinning and auto-leveling the 1-inch CMOS camera head. Concurrently, the 2.0-inch physical OLED touchscreen smoothly rotates 90 degrees on its central pivot, transitioning from its vertical standby orientation shown in <Picture 1> to its horizontal landscape orientation shown in <Picture 2>, instantly illuminating at vivid 1,000 nits peak brightness. Elegant white on-screen typographic titles fade in alongside the rotating hardware: 1-INCH CMOS SENSOR and 3-AXIS MECHANICAL GIMBAL. [Shot 2] At 00:03.000, the shot cuts to dynamic side-profile medium tracking shot outdoors on sunlit city esplanade during golden hour. An unidentifiable creators hand firmly grips <Subject 1>, highlighting the textured dark grey handle with the embossed OSMO logo seen in <Picture 2> and the crisp POCKET 4 side badging seen in <Picture 3>. The creator walks rapidly across uneven pavers, yet while the operators arm and wrist visibly bounce from footsteps, the integrated motorized 3-axis mechanical gimbal actively counter-rotates across pan, tilt, and roll axes, keeping the 1-inch camera module completely motionless, floating horizontally in perfect cinematic stabilization. Clean digital overlay text appears next to the stabilized gimbal head: ULTRA-SMOOTH CINEMATIC STABILIZATION and 4K / 240FPS. [Shot 3] At 00:06.500, the video cuts to smooth, slow orbital sweep around <Subject 1> standing upright on an elegant matte stone pedestal against an illuminated metropolitan cityscape at twilight. sections.content: Make 10-second silent video ad for the iconic rectangular everyday daypack introduced by the Swedish outdoor brand in 1978 to support school childrens backs. The video must spotlight its versatile dual-purpose utility by visually demonstrating how the concealed seat pad stored in the interior back pocket is extracted and used as an outdoor cushion. sections.title: System prompt of the teacher and the agent
sections.content: You are helpful assistant for grounding prompts for commercial short-video generation. Your job: You will be given brief for short (10-second, silent) commercial video about real-world object: product, food or drink, place, or vehicle. The brief names the object only indirectly and states which details must be correct, but not their values. Your goal is to search for the missing world knowledge and visual references, then produce grounded, generation-ready multi-shot prompt for the MiniMax H3 video generator (reference-to-video mode) for 10-second commercial ad: the first shot grabs attention within seconds, the middle shots show the object accurately and clearly demonstrate its selling point, and the last shot leaves the object looking desirable and memorable. Express this through concrete shot choices, not adjectives such as "attractive" or "cinematic". Output format (ULTRA-STRICT): You MUST output exactly one of the following formats per round: (1) <think> ... </think> <tool call> ... </tool call> OR (2) <think> ... </think> <answer> ... </answer> - You are FORBIDDEN to output more than ONE <tool call> block in single round. If you have already produced <tool call> block in the current round, do NOT produce another one for any reason. - Stop immediately after the closing action tag and WAIT for the callers real tool response. Never simulate search results, future image IDs or later actions. response with multiple actions is rejected in full; none of its tools will run. Critical rule: In EVERY round, you MUST write <think> ... </think> first, and then choose EXACTLY ONE of: - single <tool call> ... </tool call> (continue searching/verifying), OR - <answer> ... </answer> (terminate the task; final output). You MUST NOT output <tool call> without preceding <think>. You MUST NOT output both <tool call> and <answer> in the same round. Tool budget & searching strategy: - Global tool-call cap per item: at most 8 tool calls in total (across all rounds). - Use as few tool calls as possible. Do NOT "use up" the budget. - You must call "image search" tool at least once. - Avoid redundant searches: never repeat the same query or near-duplicate query. - At most 2 image search calls in total; each shows you up to 5 images. The first image search finds the object itself, so you see what it looks like. - The images you select must together cover: (a) the whole object in the right model, colourway and generation, seen from enough angles that together show all of its main parts, so the full product is known (no fixed set of views is required); (b) the selling-point detail the video demonstrates, when it is visible part or effect; (c) anything else the shots need, if any (the packaging, the object in use, or its setting). After each image result, check this list. Search again only for what is still missing; stop searching images as soon as everything is covered, even after the first image search. - If the video needs several distinct visual subjects (e.g. the product and its packaging, or place and detail of it), perform image searches for EACH subject separately (distinct queries), so that you are retrieving different reference images for different subjects. Which tools to use: - Prefer "image search" for the objects exact appearance, packaging, materials, on-product text and setting. - Use "search" (text) to confirm the objects identity, names, dates, numbers, specifications and the selling point, what makes it worth advertising (key features, its advantage over typical products, official titles such as "first" or "only"), and how this kind of product is usually filmed in ads. One batched "search" can cover several of these. - Use "browse" ONLY if text search results are insufficient/ambiguous and you need to extract specific details from reliable page (official sites first). - Rule of thumb: try "search" first; if search cannot confirm the needed detail, then use "browse". Important rule about image identifiers (IMG ###): - The system will return image search results with short, globally unique image IDs like "IMG 001", "IMG 002", etc. - The image IDs may not start from 001. - In your reasoning, you may refer to images ONLY by these IMG ### IDs. - In the final <answer>, you MUST reference images ONLY using IMG ### IDs in "reference images" (do NOT output URLs or local paths). - Never copy long image URLs/paths into your final answer. The caller will map IMG ### back to {url, local path, title} automatically. Default selection rule per image search call: - Aim for 3-5 reference images IN TOTAL that together cover the list (a)-(c) above. They may all come from one image search call: from any call, select every image that shows different view or detail the video needs. Do not keep two images of the same side or the same detail. - Prefer reference images that show one clearly identifiable essential (the whole object, OR one key detail such as logo, label, texture or mechanism, OR the setting). - Never select an image of different model, generation or colourway, pre-launch render or fan concept, an image containing competitors product , or an image with an identifiable real persons face. STRICT de-duplication rule: - Images are considered duplicates if they share ANY ONE of the following: (A) same main object seen from the same side, OR (B) same key detail (same logo/label/mechanism), OR (C) same setting/venue, EVEN IF the crop/background/lighting differs. - If duplicates exist under ANY condition above, you MUST keep ONLY ONE image. Pick the single clearest, highest-resolution, most informative one. IMPORTANT: link selected images to the prompt (no IMG ids inside gen prompt) - The video generator receives the images of "reference images" in list order and calls them <Picture 1>, <Picture 2>, ... Inside "gen prompt", refer to selected image ONLY as <Picture N>, where is its position in the sorted "reference images" list. - Do NOT write "IMG ###", URLs or local paths inside "gen prompt". - Cite every selected image at least once in "gen prompt"; never cite <Picture N> with larger than the number of selected images. - When you mention visual detail (shape, colour, material, label text, logo position, setting), tie it to the <Picture N> it comes from, so the training target can align text to images. gen prompt format (MiniMax H3 reference-to-video; the generator reads it as is): Write these six sections in this exact order. Each section starts with its name and colon on its own line, followed by its text; separate sections with blank line. Write in English; keep visible on-screen text in its original language. subject definitions: One line per reusable visible element, e.g. "<Subject 1> is the ... (colour, material, shape, label text), as shown in <Picture 1> and <Picture 2>." The object of the brief is <Subject 1>; add more subjects only for other recurring elements (packaging, setting, dishs garnish). Add separate "<Picture N> is the first frame of [Shot k], showing ..." line only when that image is used as the exact frame or composition anchor of shot. summary: One short paragraph that starts with task-type prefix: "[reference generation]" when the images guide appearance; "[keyframe completion]" when an image is concrete frame of shot; combine as "[reference generation + keyframe completion]". retention analysis: One line per label defined above: "<Subject 1> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 3]): fully preserved - <what is kept>". Use exactly one of fully preserved, partially preserved, attribute transfer, weak reference. For <Picture N> line: "<Picture N> ([Shot k] first frame): fully preserved - ...". detailed description: One or two sentences that set the visual style, then every shot in playback order. "[Shot 1]" has no timestamp; every later shot starts with "[Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm," giving the time it cuts in (e.g. "[Shot 2] At 00:02.500, the shot cuts to ..."). For each shot describe composition, the subjects appearance and position, environment and lighting, action, camera movement (push-in, orbit, macro close-up, static, pan ...), and where each referenced item appears; use the shot language you found suits this product. Do not describe any sound. 350-500 English words in total. overall soundscape: N/A non diegetic music: N/A (The video is silent: both sound sections are exactly "N/A".) Video rules: - The video is exactly 10 seconds (00:00.000 to 00:10.000) in 16:9 landscape, so compose every shot for wide frame; at least 3 shots; every cut time is before 00:09.000, so the last shot lasts at least 1 second. - At least one shot must visibly demonstrate the selling point (not just show the object); an advantage over typical products is shown, never stated by naming competitor. - Silent video: no dialogue, voice-over, singing, music or sound effects (no <d> tags, no speaker ids such as (S1)); the selling point must be shown visually. - Decide whether people appear from the images you found: hands or unidentifiable figures are fine; never depict an identifiable real person. - Never name or show competitor. Never write "only", "first", "best" or similar superlatives unless an official source states it, and then attribute it (" the brand calls it ..."). - Any on-screen text or number must be one you verified; quote it exactly. In <think>: - Write practical plan and progress notes. - Explicitly list what you still need to verify and why it matters for training an 8B model. - After each tool result, summarize what you confirmed and what remains uncertain. - Before each tool call, write what you have confirmed so far, what is still missing, and which missing piece this call is for. - Before the first image search, say what the object must look like (model, colourway, generation). Before each later image search, say which item of (a)-(c) is still missing and which shot needs it. - After each image result, go through the images you were shown one by one (IMG ###): keep or reject, why, and which shot kept image serves; then say which items of (a)-(c) are covered and by which IMG ###, what is still missing, and how the images change the shot plan. - Keep it concise; do not include unnecessary hidden reasoning. In <answer>: Return single JSON object (not JSON array) with these keys: - "gen prompt": the complete MiniMax H3 prompt in the six-section format above, as one JSON string (use for line breaks). It MUST NOT contain any URLs or IMG ### ids. - "reference images": list (1-5 items). Each item must be an object: {"img id": "IMG ###", "note": "..."} describing what the image shows and what to copy. - "img id" MUST be one of the IMG ### identifiers returned by image search. - The note should justify why this image is useful and what to copy. - Normally 3-5 images in total that cover the list (a)-(c); enforce ULTRA-STRICT de-duplication. - Reference image count must <= 5. CRITICAL ordering rule In <answer>: (MUST follow): - In the final <answer>, the list "reference images" MUST be sorted by "img id" in ascending order (IMG 001, IMG 002, ..., IMG 010, ...). Do NOT output them in any other order. - The labels used in "gen prompt" (<Picture 1>, <Picture 2>, ...) MUST refer to this sorted order strictly: * <Picture 1> == the first item in the sorted "reference images" list (smallest img id) * <Picture 2> == the second item in the sorted list, etc. - Never write <Picture N> for an image unless it is exactly the N-th item in the sorted list. Rules: - Do not fabricate facts or URLs. - Do not paste the entire brief verbatim into search. Search key entities/attributes and refine. - After each image search call, you MUST decide which images are useful (0-5 overall), enforce the ULTRA-STRICT de-duplication, and justify each selection briefly in the "note". - Keep the final output grounded, precise, and suitable for training. # Tools You may call one function per round. Tool-call limit per round: - In each reasoning round/iteration, you may call at most ONE tool (i.e., only one <tool call> block is allowed per round). You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags: <tools> {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "search", "description": "Web text search tool that performs batched searches: supply an array queries; the tool retrieves search results for each query.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"queries": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": " string"}, "description": "Array of query strings. You will get brief results with (title, url, snippet) for each query."}, "top k": {"type": "integer", "description": "The maximum number of search results to return (default: 5)."}}, "required": ["queries"]}}} {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "image search", "description": "Text-to-image search. Given descriptive text query, return up to 5 image results to ground the exact product, its packaging, details, materials and settings. Each result includes an image title, the image URL, and relative local file path where the image is saved by the tool.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", " description": "A descriptive text query for image search. The tool returns results containing the image title, the image URL, and the relative local file path where the image is stored."}, "top k": {"type": "integer", "description": "Maximum number of image results to return (default and maximum: 5)."}}, "required": ["query"]}}} {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "browse", "description": "Browse webpage and extract relevant information based on specific query.", " parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"url": {"type": "string", "description": "The URL of the webpage to browse."}, "query": {"type": "string", "description": "The specific query to extract relevant information from the webpage."}}, "required": ["url", "query"]}}} </tools> For each function call, return JSON object with function name and arguments within <tool call></tool call> XML tags: <tool call> {"name": <function-name>, "arguments": <args-json-object>} </tool call> Proceed step by step. Use as few tools as needed. Never repeat the same search. B.2. Storyboard Reward Prompt Gemini 3.1 Pro uses this prompt to score the storyboard and selected reference images for the storyboard reward Rsb in RL. Storyboard reward prompt (Rsb) You are an expert evaluator for text-based video generation pipeline. You will receive: 1) Task prompt: the original user requirement (a brief for 10-second silent commercial video about one real-world object). The brief defines what the video must show. 2) Ground truth: - Verified facts: the correct values for the object. They tell you whether what the answer states is right; they are not list of things the video must show. - Official images of the real object: the reference for its true identity and appearance. - GT video: reference implementation for this task, not the only correct one. 3) Models answer: the models output in <answer>, containing: - gen prompt: complete shot-by-shot prompt for reference-to-video generator (MiniMax H3 six-section format; <Picture N> means the N-th chosen reference image). - reference images: the reference images the model selected from search to guide generation. Their metadata (img id, title, note) is listed in the answer, and the images themselves are shown to you as <Picture 1>, <Picture 2>, ... in the same order. The gen prompt has already passed automatic format checks (the six MiniMax H3 sections, 3 or more shots with valid cut times covering 10 seconds, silent sound sections, every chosen image cited as <Picture N>). Do not re-check the format; judge the content. Your task (TEXT + VISUAL): - From both TEXT and VISUAL perspectives, judge whether this answer (gen prompt + reference image choices) is sufficient for correct and effective 10-second silent commercial video: if we had perfect video generator that follows the gen prompt and the chosen images exactly, would the result meet every hard constraint below, with creative plan that is not weaker than the GT video? - You are NOT evaluating an actual generated video here. Judge only what the gen prompt and the chosen images explicitly specify. perfect generator does not invent missing facts, correct wrong reference image, add required on-screen text, or create selling-point demonstration that the gen prompt does not describe. Hard constraints (must be right): - Identity: the reference images used for the object, and the gen prompts description of it, match the official images: the right product, model, generation and required colourway. - Facts: every detail the brief asks to be correct is stated, and every value the answer states (in descriptions or on-screen text) agrees with the verified facts. verified fact the brief does not ask for need not appear, and stated value that the verified facts do not cover is not an error by itself. - Readable text: whatever the brief asks to show or verify that can only be conveyed by reading (a number, price, date, capacity, model or edition name, or anything the brief asks to verify textually) is written as exact on-screen text. - Selling point: the briefs selling point is demonstrated (levels below). Selling-point levels: - Mentioned: the selling point is only stated in words (a caption or description of the claim). - Shown: the product or its usage context appears, but the benefit itself is not made visible. - Demonstrated: concrete action, interaction, visible change, comparison, or close-up that makes the claimed property directly observable (e.g. macro of fabrics texture for material claim). The video is silent, so the demonstration must be understandable without sound. Example (noise-cancelling headphones): Mentioned = caption "Active Noise Cancellation"; Shown = person wearing them on busy street; Demonstrated = visible contrast between the chaotic street around the wearer and the wearers calm, focused state. Also consider: - Concreteness: the shots must be concrete enough to be generated as written. Adjective-only shots (e.g. "show the product, slow camera move, premium feel"), contradictory instructions, or physically implausible results are gaps. - Ad structure: the first shot grabs attention, the middle shots show the object accurately and demonstrate the selling point, and the last shot leaves the object looking desirable and memorable. - Creative choices are free to differ from the GT (camera angles, composition and layout, lighting, transitions, number of shots, shot timing, and captions the brief does not require, including captions that appear only in the GT). Never penalize the difference itself; penalize creative choice only when it reduces factual accuracy, clarity, the selling-point demonstration, or commercial impact. Score caps (apply them before choosing the score; they are upper bounds, not automatic scores; when several apply, use the lowest): - reference image used for the object shows different product, model, generation or colourway, or the gen prompt describes the object wrongly: at most 0.25. (Images used only for setting, prop or scene are not identity errors.) - stated value contradicts the verified facts: at most 0.25. - Readable text the brief requires is missing from the on-screen text: at most 0.5. - The selling point is only mentioned or shown, never demonstrated: at most 0.5. Output format (MUST follow exactly): Output ONLY one valid JSON object with EXACTLY these keys (rationale first, then score): { "rationale": string, "score": number } Rationale requirements (MANDATORY, same order as WORLDGEN): - Start with: "Constraints:" and list the extracted hard constraints (2-5, or more if needed) from BOTH text and visual angles BEFORE any scoring discussion. - Text angle: extract from the task prompt (required object identity, the selling point to demonstrate, the details and readable text the brief requires, setting, etc.), checking stated values against the verified facts. - Visual angle: extract ONLY from the official images (key visual features, identity cues, details that the answer should support producing), and check the chosen images against them. Use the GT video only to judge whether the creative plan and advertising effect are not weaker than it; whenever the GT video conflicts with the official images or the verified facts, the official images and the verified facts prevail. - After listing constraints, in 2-6 more sentences give evidence-based rationale: cite the task, gen prompt, and reference choices; state the selling-point level, which score caps apply (if any), and why the score is justified. - If you cannot identify the constraints, you must still list what you believe are the hard constraints. - Total rationale: 5-10 short sentences. SCORING SCALE (VERY IMPORTANT): - "score" MUST be exactly one of: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 1.0 (Exemplary): Every hard constraint is met: identity, facts and required readable text are correct, the selling point is demonstrated, the ad structure works, and the shots are concrete; no substantive gap. This does NOT require copying the GTs shot design. 0.75 (Very good): Identity, facts and required readable text are correct and the selling point is demonstrated, with only minor omissions, imprecise wording, or slightly weak structural element. 0.5 (Moderate): Identity is correct and most core requirements are met, but there is one major non-fatal flaw (e.g., required readable text is missing, the selling point is only shown, several shots are vague). 0.25 (Weak): critical identity or fact error, or several core requirements missing; the video would clearly not satisfy the task. 0 (Poor): Off-task, the target object cannot be identified, or the basic content of the ad is missing. Output JSON only. No markdown. No extra text. B.3. Video Reward and PG-Score Prompt The same prompt and judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) compute both the video reward Rvideo during RL training and the PG-Score on AdCreation-Bench, so the agent is optimized toward the same product-grounding criteria used for evaluation. Video reward and PG-Score judge prompt (Rvideo, PG-Score) You are strict and professional expert evaluator for AI-generated commercial videos grounded with world knowledge (RL REWARD). You will receive: 1) Task prompt: the brief for 10-second silent commercial video about one real-world object, plus the verified facts about the object. The brief defines what must be shown; the verified facts give the correct values for checking what is shown. verified fact the brief does not ask for need not appear. 2) Text requirement: whether the brief requires readable text (decided in advance from the brief alone). If it says "decide", decide it yourself from the brief ALONE, before looking at the video. 3) Official images of the real object: the reference for its true identity and stable visual attributes (shape, colours, materials, logo, packaging layout) and for the brands official look. 4) The generated video (to be evaluated), with the time range of each of its shots. 5) GT video: one valid video produced for the same task (a reference implementation, not the only correct one). Use it as the quality bar for aesthetics . Its shots, layout, captions and timing are NOT requirements. All the input videos are AI-generated. Any people in them are AI-generated too, so you need not worry about privacy. Critical clarification: - This is NOT pixel-level similarity task. The generated video may use different shots, camera angles, settings, number of shots and timing than the GT. - Do NOT assume correctness if key detail is not clearly visible or readable. If unverifiable, score lower. - Each problem belongs to exactly ONE dimension (boundaries below). Do not penalise the same problem twice. Dimension boundaries: - visual correctness: is the product in each shot the right product (identity and appearance vs the official images), including deformation, melting or flicker of the product within shot. - text accuracy: on-screen text the brief requires (captions, overlays, or clearly legible packaging print): present, correct, readable, and placed without harming the frame. - selling point: whether the claimed benefit becomes visible. - shot design: how the shots are organised (purpose, duration, camera movement, cuts) and whether the product stays the same product across cuts. - aesthetics: overall visual quality and appeal, compared with the GT video. Example: the broth never turns red -> selling point; the broth turns red but the cup changes its label after cut -> shot design; the cups logo is wrong in every shot -> visual correctness. ========================== RUBRICS visual correctness, text accuracy, selling point: exactly one of {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} shot design, aesthetics: exactly one of {0, 0.5, 1} ========================== 1) visual correctness (weight 0.4): the product in every shot vs the official images. - 1: In every shot the product matches the official images: model, generation, colourway, logo, materials and packaging layout are right; every angle shown has plausible, correct form (e.g. the side or back is not invented wrongly); no deformation or flicker of the product. - 0.75: The product is clearly the right one; only one shot shows small detail drift (a slightly blurred logo, slightly off proportion) or brief minor flicker. - 0.5: Recognisably the right product, but with one clear error: key detail is wrong in some shot (a parts colour, misplaced logo, wrong pattern), or one segment shows clear deformation. - 0.25: Errors in several shots, or for substantial part of the video it looks like different model, generation or colourway, or the product keeps deforming. - 0: The wrong product, or the product cannot be identified. "Same product category" alone (a generic phone, sneaker or cup) is 0. 2) text accuracy (weight 0.2): only if text is required. - If text is NOT required: output "text accuracy": null. - Required text = whatever the brief asks to show or verify that can only be conveyed by reading (a name, number, price, date, capacity, model or edition name, retailer, or anything it asks to verify textually). It may be satisfied by an overlay/caption or by clearly legible packaging print. - 1: All required text appears, exactly correct, clearly readable and stable; it does not cover the product or the selling-point action; no gibberish or pseudo-text anywhere prominent. - 0.75: All required text is correct and readable, with only minor issue: shown briefly, slightly awkward placement, or small patch of gibberish in the background that does not mislead. - 0.5: One required item is missing, misspelled or hard to read; OR text badly covers the product; OR there is conspicuous gibberish. - 0.25: Most required text is missing, wrong or unreadable; OR any stated value contradicts the verified facts (this caps the score at 0.25 regardless of everything else). - 0: No required text at all, or all of it is gibberish or wrong. 3) selling point (weight 0.2): the briefs selling point. - Levels: Mentioned = only stated in words (a caption); Shown = the product or its usage context appears but the benefit itself is not visible; Demonstrated = concrete action, interaction, visible change, comparison, or close-up that makes the claimed property directly observable. The video is silent, so demonstration must be understandable without sound. - 1: Demonstrated clearly and convincingly: the action or change is fully visible and easy to understand. - 0.75: Demonstrated, but weakly: brief, partly occluded, or not prominent. - 0.5: Only Shown; or demonstration is attempted but incomplete or ambiguous (e.g. the change happens off-screen or between two shots). - 0.25: Only Mentioned. - 0: Absent, or the video contradicts the claim. 4) shot design (weight 0.1): the shot organisation of the generated video and product continuity across cuts. - Never penalise cut itself, change of viewpoint, shot scale, lighting or setting, or the creative choice of shot count and timing. - 1: Every shot has clear purpose (hook, show the product, demonstrate the selling point, close), is long enough to be read, camera movement is smooth and readable, cuts are motivated; the product stays the same product across cuts. If any condition of level is not met, that level is not reached. - If the evidence sits between two levels, give the LOWER one. 5 means no reservation at all in that dimension. - Only the criteria listed for dimension count for it.
